newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French Axa, UAP merge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French Axa, UAP merge.

text.p: French insurers Axa and Union des Assurances de Paris said on Tuesday they were merging to create a world leader in insurance.
"This projected alliance presents both companies with a unique opportunity to create an asset management group which will enjoy an unparalleled strategic position," they said in a joint statement.
Details of the offer, which took many analysts by surprise despite renewed market speculation last week of a takeover by Axa, were due to be revealed at a 1200 GMT news conference.
A UAP-Axa merger would create a group that would rival Nippon Life, the world's biggest insurance company.
Market sources said they were expecting a merger to be made on the basis of two Axa shares for five UAP shares and they also raised the possibility of a cash option.
The boards of the two companies, second and third biggest in Europe in terms of sales behind Germany's Allianz, were meeting to discuss the deal on Tuesday and trading in their shares was suspended.
Talk of an Axa takeover has been pushing UAP shares up recently. The UAP share closed at its highest level since early March on Friday, up 6.27 percent at 116.90 francs.
UAP was privatised in 1994 at 152 francs a share and hit a high of 160 francs in July of the same year before a decline.
Axa, whose stock closed on Friday at 318.5 francs, has a strong presence outside France, notably in the United States, where it owns Equitable and National Mutual in Australia.

Axa reported first-half net attributable profit of 1.977 billion francs ($390 million) on turnover of 87.5 billion francs, while UAP emerged from a two billion franc loss in 1995 to produce a first-half 1996 net attributable profit of 860 million francs.
Analysts said after news of the alliance emerged that they were waiting to see how the two reorganise their businesses, particularly in France.
They noted the merger would give Axa access to the German market through UAP's German subsidiary Colonia AG.
"It gives Axa a good German business," UBS Phillips & Drew insurance analyst Andrew Goodwin said. "The question is what Axa and UAP together can do in France," he said.

On Friday, analysts had said UAP would be an improbable fit for Axa, which has built a worldwide presence through its 1991 acquisition of Equitable Cos of the United States and purchase last year of a 51 percent stake in Australia's second largest life insurer, National Mutual.
"It does take Axa more back into Europe and more back into non-life," Goodwin said.
Besides access to Germany, however, the merger would also boost Axa's position in France, where it is the country's second biggest insurer behind UAP.
"Axa feels its home base is not as strong as it would like it to be," one analyst, who declined to be named, said.
He noted that UAP's insurance premiums worldwide were around 50 percent bigger than those of Axa.

"I am surprised that it has happened so quickly. On an industrial level, it seems reasonable. It will create a fairly balanced group, with, however, a few overlaps in Europe, especially in France," Claudie Casimir, analysts at brokers Massonaud said.
All were in little doubt that it would be Axa which dominated the new merged company.
"It is clear that Axa is taking the lead," another analyst, who declined to be named, said.
Some said they were surprised that UAP would be willing to go along with the merger just after recovering from the weight of hefty property provisions. ($1=5.057 French Franc)
